01.event: Rav Ashi visited Rav Kahana's house for a wedding and recited the wedding blessings over the following days.
01.turn: After the first day he recited all seven blessings only when new faces were present; otherwise he treated it as a continuation of the celebration and said only two.
01.summary: Rav Ashi came to Rav Kahana's house during a wedding celebration. On the first day he recited all seven wedding blessings. On later days he recited all of them only if new guests had come; otherwise he said just the blessing 'In Whose dwelling is joy' and 'Who has created', since it was merely an extension of the celebration.
01.missing: The passage describes his practice over several days rather than a single turning point or ending.

02.event: The two schools disputed for two and a half years whether it is better for man to have been created or not.
02.outcome: They concluded it would have been better for man not to have been created, but now that he exists he should examine his deeds.
02.summary: For two and a half years the schools of Shammai and Hillel argued whether it would have been better for humanity never to have been created. Finally they took a vote and decided it would have been better not to be created. Since man has been created, however, he should examine his actions.
02.missing: The dispute is reported as a debate and verdict, without any particular scene or actors.

03.actor: A dying man, his daughter and heirs; Rav Ashi
03.event: A man willed a palm tree to his daughter but left only two half-shares of palm trees, which the heirs wanted to give her.
03.turn: Rav Ashi was unsure whether two halves of palm trees count as 'a palm tree'.
03.outcome: Rav Mordekhai cited Rava that people do call two halves a palm tree, so the heirs could give her the two halves.
03.summary: A man wrote in his will that his daughter should get a palm tree, but when he died he owned only half-shares in two trees. The heirs wanted to give her the two halves. Rav Ashi wondered whether two half-trees really count as 'a palm tree'; Rav Mordekhai told him, in Rava's name, that people do speak that way, so the halves sufficed.

04.event: Villagers asked Rabbi Yirmeya whether an eiruv may be made with moist beans.
04.turn: He did not know the answer.
04.outcome: Back at the study hall he was told Rabbi Yannai permitted it, with Rav Yehiel giving the amount as a handful.
04.summary: Rabbi Yirmeya visited some villages, and the people asked him whether they could make an eiruv with moist beans. He had no answer. When he returned to the study hall, the scholars told him Rabbi Yannai had ruled it permitted, and Rav Yehiel said a handful is needed.

05.event: He performed a halitza with a non-leather slipper, alone as sole judge, at night.
05.turn: Shmuel criticized him for relying on individual minority opinions.
05.outcome: Shmuel's sarcastic rebuke stands as the verdict on his conduct.
05.summary: Rabba bar Hiyya from Ctesiphon conducted a halitza ceremony using a slipper rather than a leather shoe, as the only judge, and at night. Shmuel scoffed at him, saying how bold he was to follow individual opinions not accepted as law.

06.actor: Rav Aha bar Abba and Rav Hisda
06.event: Rav Aha bar Abba visited his son-in-law Rav Hisda and sat his granddaughter on his lap.
06.turn: Rav Hisda objected that she might be betrothed; they traded accusations of violating rulings of Rav and Shmuel.
06.outcome: Rav Aha answered that he follows Shmuel's other ruling: all is permitted for the sake of Heaven.
06.summary: Rav Aha bar Abba came to visit his son-in-law Rav Hisda and put his granddaughter on his lap. Rav Hisda asked whether he didn't think she might already be betrothed. Rav Aha retorted that betrothing a minor daughter would itself break Rav's ruling; Rav Hisda answered that holding a woman breaks Shmuel's ruling. Rav Aha replied that he follows another teaching of Shmuel: everything done for the sake of Heaven is permitted.

07.event: The people of the Galilee asked Rabbi Helbo who reads from the Torah after the priest and Levite.
07.turn: He did not know the answer.
07.outcome: He asked Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha, who gave the order: scholars who are communal leaders, then scholars fit to lead, then their sons, then synagogue heads and anyone.
07.summary: The Galileans sent Rabbi Helbo a question: after the priest and Levite, who should be called to the Torah? He did not know, so he went and asked Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha. Rabbi Yitzhak told him the order: scholars appointed as community leaders, then scholars fit to be appointed, then sons of such leaders, then heads of synagogues and finally anyone.

08.actor: Ameimar, a woman and her brothers (reported by Rav Minyumi)
08.event: A woman came before Ameimar claiming a tenth of her father's estate.
08.turn: Her brothers said that if they had money they would pay her off in cash, and Ameimar said nothing against it.
08.outcome: His silence showed he had come to regard a daughter as a creditor who can be paid in cash, retracting his earlier view.
08.summary: Rav Minyumi recalled standing before Ameimar when a woman came asking for a tenth of her father's estate as her dowry. Her brothers told her that if they had the money they would simply pay her off in cash. Ameimar remained silent and did not object, which Rav Minyumi took as a sign that Ameimar had changed his mind and now treated the daughter as a creditor rather than an heir.

09.actor: A half-slave half-free woman and her master
09.event: The court forced the master of a half-slave half-free woman to free her.
09.summary: A woman who was half slave and half free was in a situation where the court compelled her master to set her fully free, and he did so. The Gemara then debates why: either because women are obligated to procreate, or because men were taking liberties with her.
09.missing: The reason for the coercion is not stated in the incident itself; it is only argued about afterward.

10.event: A man passed by the entrance of his father-in-law's house and Rav Sheshet had him lashed.
10.turn: It is explained that the man was suspected of an affair with his mother-in-law.
10.summary: A man merely passed by the door of his father-in-law's house, and Rav Sheshet had him flogged. The reason was that the man was rumored to be involved with his mother-in-law, so even passing near the house lent credence to the rumor.
10.missing: The incident is cited briefly inside a legal argument; the explanation is the Gemara's, not part of a told scene.

11.event: In a case where a creditor forgave a sold debt, Rafram pressed Rav Ashi to rule.
11.turn: Rav Ashi ruled the creditor liable for indirect damage.
11.outcome: He made the creditor pay the full value of the note.
11.summary: A case came up in which a creditor voided a promissory note he had sold. Rafram pressed Rav Ashi to give a definite ruling, and Rav Ashi made the creditor pay the full amount of the debt, as if he had destroyed a valuable beam meant for a sculpture.
11.missing: The facts of the case are given only by reference to the preceding legal discussion.

12.actor: A yevama and yavam; Rabbi Akiva
12.event: A couple performed halitza privately in prison, and the case came before Rabbi Akiva, who was imprisoned.
12.turn: The question is how anyone knew what happened between them; witnesses watched from outside.
12.summary: A man and woman performed halitza by themselves while in prison, and the case was brought to Rabbi Akiva, who was himself imprisoned. He validated it. The Gemara explains that witnesses had watched from outside, and that both the ceremony and the ruling took place in prison.
12.missing: The incident itself is in the Mishna, which is only referred to, not shown.

14.event: Rabbi went to study Torah with Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua.
14.turn: The students ganged up on him like aggressive roosters and would not let him learn.
14.outcome: He learned only one teaching: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that intercourse with a hermaphrodite incurs stoning as with a male.
14.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi recalled going to study with Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua. The other students banded together against him like the fierce roosters of Beit Bukya and would not let him study there. In the end he came away with only one teaching from the Mishna: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling about a hermaphrodite.

15.actor: Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of Dabil; Shmuel
15.event: Rav Yosef ruled in a betrothal case following Rav rather than Shmuel.
15.turn: Shmuel took offense and sarcastically asked whether this scholar had been given a bigger measure of wisdom than everyone else.
15.summary: Rav Yosef of Dabil ruled in an actual case according to Rav's view, disregarding the father's betrothal. Shmuel was offended and sarcastically remarked that wisdom seems to have been measured out to everyone in a small measure but to this man in a large one.
15.missing: The facts of the case and any resolution are not told; the incident is cited as evidence in an argument.

16.actor: Rava and Rav Natan bar Ami
16.event: Rava compelled the wealthy Rav Natan bar Ami to give charity.
16.outcome: Rava collected four hundred zuz from him for charity.
16.summary: Rava forced Rav Natan bar Ami, a wealthy man, to contribute to charity and took four hundred zuz from him for that purpose.
16.missing: No circumstances or reaction are given; it is a bare report cited as precedent.

17.event: A childless woman came before Rabbi Ami demanding her marriage-contract payment and a divorce.
17.turn: He told her she was not commanded to have children; she answered that she needed children to care for her in old age.
17.outcome: Rabbi Ami ruled that in such a case the husband is forced to divorce her.
17.summary: A woman whose husband could not father children came to Rabbi Ami and asked for her marriage-contract money. He sent her away, saying women are not commanded to have children. She replied: who will care for this woman in her old age? Persuaded, Rabbi Ami ruled that in such a case the husband must be compelled to divorce her.

18.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya and a heretic
18.event: A heretic mocked Rabbi Yehoshua as a 'man of thorns', citing Micah's 'the best of them is as a brier'.
18.turn: Rabbi Yehoshua called him a fool and pointed to the end of the verse.
18.outcome: He reinterpreted the verse as praise: the righteous protect Israel like a thorn hedge, or crush the nations.
18.summary: A heretic taunted Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya, calling him a 'man of thorns' because the prophet says the best of Israel are like briers. Rabbi Yehoshua called him a fool and told him to read the rest of the verse. He explained that the verse is praise: just as thorns seal a breach, the best among Israel protect it.

20.event: A student of Rabbi Eliezer became liable to death by burning for his sins.
20.turn: The Sages said to leave him alone because he had served a great man.
20.summary: One of Rabbi Eliezer's students committed a sin deserving death by burning. The Sages decided to leave him unpunished, because he had served a great teacher.
20.missing: What he did and what happened afterward are not told.
